title: Psalm 115: Not to Us, but to Your Name
summary: Answering the taunt of the nations, “Where is their God?”, the psalm declares that Israel's God is in heaven and does as he pleases, while idols of silver and gold can neither see, hear, nor act. It calls Israel, the priests, and all who fear the LORD to trust him, promises his blessing on small and great alike, and ends with the living vowing to bless the LORD forever.
story: Psalm 115 is the third psalm of the Egyptian Hallel (113 to 118). After Psalm 114 recalled the exodus, when God's power was plain to see, Psalm 115 faces a time when the nations can mock Israel by asking where its God has gone. That question fits the long years after the exile, when Israel was small and dominated by empires full of splendid temples and images. The psalm answers not by pointing to Israel's strength but by giving all glory to God's name and exposing the emptiness of the idols.
historical:
The psalm has no heading. Many scholars date it after the exile because of the nations' taunt, which also appears in Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17 in contexts of national humiliation, and because its mockery of idols is close to Isaiah 44:9-20 and Jeremiah 10:1-16. Others place it in any period when Israel faced defeat. Its three-fold call in verses 9 to 13 to Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD suggests a temple liturgy, perhaps with a leader's call and a choir's response. Verses 4 to 8 appear again almost word for word in Psalm 135:15-18.

In the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) and some Hebrew manuscripts this psalm is joined to Psalm 114 as a single psalm. The group called those who fear the LORD has been understood in two ways: as a summary of all Israel after naming its laity and priests, or as Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God without full conversion, a group well known in later centuries. Both readings are held by careful interpreters.
cultural:
Idols in the ancient Near East were not thought of by their worshipers as mere statues. Temples held carefully made images, often of wood overlaid with gold and silver, which were ritually consecrated through ceremonies in Mesopotamia and Egypt meant to open their mouths, eyes, and ears so that the god could dwell in them. Priests fed, clothed, and washed them daily. The psalm's list of mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see, and ears that cannot hear is a direct mockery of that belief. The final insult is that idols cannot even clear their throats.

The verse about the dead reflects Israel's common view of the grave in much of the Old Testament: the dead go down to silence, to Sheol, where they no longer join in the worship of the temple. The psalm uses this to press the urgency of praise for the living, who must bless God now.
literary: The psalm moves through several voices, which suggests use in worship. Verses 1 and 2 are a communal prayer, turning away from Israel's own glory. Verses 3 to 8 contrast the living God in heaven with lifeless idols, using a long list of seven body parts that do nothing. Verses 9 to 11 repeat a call to trust three times, each with the refrain He is their help and shield. Verses 12 to 15 turn the same three groups into recipients of blessing, and verses 16 to 18 close with a reflection on heaven, earth, and the grave. The word bless occurs repeatedly at the end, so that the psalm ends with human blessing answering divine blessing.

outline.t: Glory to your name, not ours, when the nations mock
The living God and the lifeless idols
Israel, priests, and God-fearers, trust the LORD
The LORD will bless small and great
The living will bless the LORD forever

doctrines.note: The psalm exposes idols as human products that cannot help, and warns that worshipers become like what they worship: blind, deaf, and unresponsive. Anything trusted in place of God, not only a statue, shares this emptiness.
“Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases.” God's freedom is not arbitrary but the freedom of the living Creator, in contrast to idols that must be carried and served.

Three times the people are called to trust in the LORD, who is their help and shield. Trust is the right response to a God who is alive and acts, and it is offered to every group from priest to newcomer.

words.note: Atsav, idol. The word is related to a root meaning to shape or fashion, and possibly to one meaning pain or toil. The psalm emphasizes that idols are shaped by human hands, the reverse of the true order in which God shapes people.

Batach, to trust, to rely on with confidence. It appears in verse 8 for those who trust idols and three times in verses 9 to 11 for trust in the LORD. The psalm asks not whether people will trust, since everyone trusts in something, but what they trust.

Magen, shield, the small round shield of a soldier. God as shield is a common image of protection in the Psalms, and here it is repeated in each call to trust, a refrain that anyone in the assembly could remember.

Barak, to bless. God blesses his people with life and increase (verses 12 to 15), and the people bless God with praise (verse 18). The same word runs in both directions, showing the exchange of gift and thanksgiving at the heart of worship.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 115 directly, so its connection to Christ is thematic. The psalm's opening refusal of glory for ourselves is the posture Jesus lived out when he sought not his own glory but the glory of the one who sent him (John 7:18). Paul's account of human idolatry in Romans 1:21-25, in which people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images, shares the psalm's diagnosis, and his proclamation that the living God has revealed himself in Jesus answers the taunt of the nations. The Christian hope of resurrection also transforms verse 17: in Christ, the dead do not remain in silence, and the living who bless the LORD now will bless him forever.

hard.q: Verse 17 says the dead do not praise the LORD. Does this psalm deny life after death?
hard.a: Much of the Old Testament speaks of the dead going down to Sheol, a shadowy place of silence cut off from the worship of the temple, and verse 17 reflects that view. Some scholars conclude that Israel for most of its history had no developed hope beyond death, and that such hope emerged only later, in texts like Daniel 12:2. Others argue that passages such as Psalm 16:10-11, Psalm 49:15, and Job 19:25-27 show hope for life with God beyond the grave even earlier. Either way, verse 17 does not say what God can do for the dead; it says that death ends a person's part in Israel's earthly worship, and it uses that fact to urge the living to praise now. Christians read it in light of the fuller revelation of the resurrection, which the New Testament grounds in Jesus' own rising from the dead: the silence of the grave is real, but it is not final.

questions: The psalm says that those who make idols become like them. What have you trusted that left you less alive and less responsive rather than more?
“Not to us, O LORD, not to us.” Where are you most tempted to seek glory for yourself in things that should point to God?
The psalm calls the small and the great alike to trust. How does God's blessing on the small challenge the way your community values people?
